dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: If the warning can be preserved, why erase the memory at all? What gives you the right to remove part of someone's history when treatment could reduce its pain without deletion?

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Today we debate whether we should erase bad memories. Cecilia argues for the motion, and Nicholas argues against it. Each opening lasts thirty seconds, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire. We finish with thirty-second closings, and I will give a ten-second cue.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Bad memories can keep fear alive long after danger has passed. Erasing them can restore sleep, trust, and a future not ruled by old pain. We should not worship suffering; when a memory harms more than it teaches, letting it go is humane.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Nicholas, over to you.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Painful memories can hurt, but they also warn us, shape judgment, and reveal what needs repair. Erasing them may offer relief while removing responsibility and useful knowledge. We should heal bad memories, not delete the evidence of what happened.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And that concludes Round one. Now we move on to Round two, and in Round two, the debaters can address one another directly. It runs two and a half minutes, starting the moment I stop. Go.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: If erasing a bad memory also removes its lesson, why call that progress? Wouldn't healing the pain while preserving the warning protect people better than deletion?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: No, erasing a bad memory need not erase its lesson; wisdom can survive without the torment attached to it. Why preserve suffering merely because it arrived carrying information?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The better policy question is how schools should teach painful history without frightening children or excusing cruelty. Should lessons use honest stories, careful guidance, and room for questions rather than forcing young minds to carry every detail?

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: We're talking about the practicality or the morality of whether we should erase painful and damaging memories.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The motion asks whether bad memories should be erased, and they should not be erased as a general remedy. We can soften their pain, but deleting them risks deleting warnings, duties, and parts of identity.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Every bad memory should be erased. If it still teaches something, we can keep the lesson without keeping the wound, so removal is the humane default.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I grant that some memories become a needless source of torment. But your default treats memory as the problem, when the real need is support, understanding, and a safe way to remember; therefore we should not erase bad memories.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: For a child, a bad memory should be preserved when it helps explain who they are. Protection can matter more than relief in that case, so erasure is not always right.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You said every bad memory should be erased, but you see it as for a child, a bad memory should be preserved.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Those statements fit because preservation can mean keeping a safe record, while erasure can mean removing the living wound. The child keeps meaning and history, but loses the torment; that is still the benefit I defend.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your compatibility claim changes the meaning of erasure. If the painful memory remains as a record, you have not erased the bad memory; you have treated it, which supports my side.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your weakest point is calling any retained record the same as retained suffering. A person can lose the fear, shame, and intrusive images while keeping a useful outline, so relief remains a form of erasure.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: A frightened child who remembers a dangerous doorway can avoid repeating the mistake. That concrete memory may protect them later, showing why deletion can create fresh danger instead of solving the original harm.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, ten seconds.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I grant that a warning can protect someone. But protection does not require reliving-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, time. And now we move on to round three. Round three, closing statements from each debater in turn. And here to make her closing statement, Cecilia.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Bad memories are not sacred simply because they are old. When they trap someone in fear, shame, or helplessness, erasing their emotional grip can restore choice and peace. Nicholas is right that lessons matter, but lessons are not the same as wounds. We can preserve meaning while removing torment, giving people a future shaped by judgment rather than injury.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds warning.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: The humane choice is not to preserve suffering for its own sake. Keep wisdom, release the wound, and let people live beyond what hurt them.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I want to go to the other side, first, Nicholas.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Relief matters, but erasure goes too far. A bad memory can carry a warning, explain a reaction, or remind us whom to protect. Cecilia's distinction between lesson and wound sounds neat, yet removing the memory can weaken both. We should face painful memories with care, support, and honest reflection. Healing changes our relationship with the past; it does not require destroying the past.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds for last word.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: A person deserves peace, but peace built on deletion can leave them less prepared and less accountable. Keep the memory, reduce its pain, and learn from what happened-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you, Nicholas. Your time is up.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you both for a thoughtful debate. This debate is now closed without declaring a winner.
